History

The bubbler sits between the dry hand pipe and the full-size bong, and it grew out of the glass pipe movement of the 1970s, when American glassblowers began making small pipes from borosilicate glass. A bubbler keeps the hand pipe's shape, a fixed bowl, a carb hole, and a mouthpiece, and adds a small built-in water chamber, so smoke passes through water like in a bong while the piece stays small enough to hold in one hand. Trade guides list the main forms as hammer, Sherlock, sidecar, pendant, concentrate, double, and ratchet bubblers, plus silicone versions, and they describe the bubbler as the everyday portable option against the bong's home use. The fixed downstem is the bubbler's defining compromise: it makes the piece simple and sturdy, and it makes cleaning harder, because nothing comes apart. Over time the same basic form was copied, adapted, and refined by many makers, so the record today covers a family of closely related objects rather than a single patented shape. Trade guides and manufacturer manuals preserve the steps of that change. The history matters because it explains why the parts are arranged the way they are: each feature survives because it solved a practical problem for the people who used the supply every day. The form changed slowly, through small improvements in materials and manufacturing rather than sudden reinvention, and each improvement can be traced in the sources cited at the end of this record. What stayed constant was the job itself, and what changed was how reliably, how evenly, and how durably that job could be done with ordinary materials and ordinary tools.

The supply in detail

The bubbler works by smoke from the fixed bowl travels down a short fixed stem below the water line in a small built-in chamber, bubbles up through the water, and is drawn to the mouthpiece, with a carb hole to clear the chamber. It is made from borosilicate glass one-piece body, fixed glass bowl and fixed downstem, water as the filtration medium, and a common example measures 130 mm long, water chamber 45 mm diameter, water depth 15 mm, bowl 18 mm diameter and 12 mm deep. The parts fit together in a fixed order, and each part has one job: to hold the material, to apply the mechanism, or to carry the result to the user. Because the parts are simple and the mechanism is mechanical or thermal rather than electronic in its basic form, the supply can be understood by inspection, measured with a ruler, and checked by the arithmetic in this record. The variants listed in the specification show how makers change size, material, and detail while keeping the same working principle, and the scale variants at the end of this record show the same design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes.

Parts and variants

Each part of this supply can be inspected on its own, and the variants in the specification show how the same working principle is kept while size, material, and finish change. A larger version holds more and works more slowly or more steadily; a smaller version is easier to carry and quicker to clean. Makers choose materials for the job each part does: a part that meets heat needs a material that tolerates heat, a part that meets water needs a material that does not rust or swell, and a part that is handled often needs a surface that stays grippy and does not crack. The scale variants at the end of this record carry that same logic further, showing the design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes, so the reader can see which dimensions change with scale and which stay the same.

Spec

Materials: Borosilicate glass one-piece body; fixed glass bowl and fixed downstem; plain water as the filtration medium

Dimensions: 130 mm long; water chamber 45 mm diameter; water depth 15 mm; bowl 18 mm diameter and 12 mm deep

Mechanism: Smoke from the fixed bowl travels down the fixed stem below the water line, bubbles up through the small water chamber, and is drawn to the mouthpiece; the carb hole is uncovered to clear the chamber

Use: Add a little water, just enough to cover the bottom of the inner stem, pack the bowl, cover the carb, light while drawing slowly, then uncover the carb and inhale

Care: Change the water after each session; shake with isopropyl alcohol and salt to clean the fixed chamber; rinse well; dry fully

Variants: Hammer bubbler; Sherlock bubbler; sidecar bubbler; pendant bubbler; concentrate bubbler; double bubbler; ratchet bubbler; silicone bubbler

Materials and design

Borosilicate glass is chosen for the bubbler because the whole piece is one fused body, and a glass that tolerates heat at the bowl and knocks in a pocket is what survives daily carrying. The wall is kept thicker around the water chamber than around the mouthpiece, because the chamber is the part that is gripped and the part that holds the water, while the mouthpiece only carries smoke. The bubbler has no joints in the usual sense: the bowl, the stem, the chamber, and the mouthpiece are fused into one piece of glass, so there is nothing to fit and nothing to leak. The outside is left smooth and clear so the water level can be read at a glance and the smoke seen moving through the chamber.

Build it yourself

A bubbler cannot be made at home: blowing a one-piece glass body with a fixed bowl, a fixed inner stem, and a carb hole is a skilled glassblowing trade, and no home method produces it safely. The closest genuine maker activity is making a padded carry case for it. Cut two pieces of thick felt or neoprene to the outline of the bubbler with a small margin, stitch or glue them together along three sides to form a pocket, and add a hook-and-loop strip to close the fourth side. Check the fit dry before any water or load goes in, and work slowly, because a build that is checked at each step is the one that works the first time it is used.

3D printing

A glass bubbler is not 3D-printable at home: no home filament prints glass, and a printed plastic body could not hold the fixed bowl or the fixed inner stem, and would soften near the heat. Print time (estimate): 1 hour 50 minutes for the cradle and 20 minutes for the cap, at the settings given. Unmodelled factors that change real print time and strength are wall thickness, supports, nozzle settings, printer motion, and material-specific slicing, and the estimate above is not a validated print job.

Use and program

Add a little water, just enough to cover the bottom of the inner stem, and check by tipping the piece gently that no water reaches the mouthpiece. Pack the bowl loosely, cover the carb with a finger, and light while drawing slowly until the chamber fills with smoke. Then uncover the carb and inhale steadily to clear the chamber. The program in this record computes the water volume in the chamber as a cylinder, the bowl cup volume as a frustum, the bowl capacity from the packing density, and the chamber volume, so the user can check that the water depth they use matches the specification and that the bowl holds the load the record claims. Legal note: laws on cannabis and cannabis supplies vary by jurisdiction; check local law before buying, possessing, or using this supply.

demo.code:
"""Demo: bubbler water, bowl, and chamber volumes — The Bubbler."""
import hashlib, math
def compute():
    ch_d = 45.0; water_h = 15.0; b_d = 18.0; b_h = 12.0; b_r = 3.0; ch_len = 60.0; rho = 0.15
    water_mm3 = math.pi * (ch_d / 2.0) ** 2 * water_h
    bowl_mm3 = math.pi * b_h / 3.0 * ((b_d / 2.0) ** 2 + (b_d / 2.0) * b_r + b_r * b_r)
    bowl_cm3 = bowl_mm3 / 1000.0
    cap = bowl_cm3 * rho
    chamber_mm3 = math.pi * (ch_d / 2.0) ** 2 * ch_len
    return {"water_volume_mL": round(water_mm3 / 1000.0, 2), "bowl_volume_cm3": round(bowl_cm3, 2), "capacity_g": round(cap, 2), "chamber_volume_mL": round(chamber_mm3 / 1000.0, 2), "bowl_diameter_mm": b_d}
def main():
    a = compute(); b = compute()
    sa = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(a.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
    sb = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(b.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
    for key in ["water_volume_mL", "bowl_volume_cm3", "capacity_g", "chamber_volume_mL", "bowl_diameter_mm"]:
        print(f"{key}: {a[key]}")
    print(f"Run 1 SHA-256: {sa}")
    print(f"Run 2 SHA-256: {sb}")
    print(f"Deterministic: {'MATCH' if sa == sb else 'MISMATCH'}")
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

materials_design: Borosilicate glass is chosen for the bubbler because the whole piece is one fused body, and a glass that tolerates heat at the bowl and knocks in a pocket is what survives daily carrying. The wall is kept thicker around the water chamber than around the mouthpiece, because the chamber is the part that is gripped and the part that holds the water, while the mouthpiece only carries smoke. Water is the filtration medium, and its depth is set by the inner stem: just enough to cover the bottom of the stem, no more, because too much water will splash into the mouthpiece when the piece is tipped. The carb hole is placed where a finger naturally rests, so the user can cover and uncover it without shifting the grip. The bubbler has no joints in the usual sense: the bowl, the stem, the chamber, and the mouthpiece are fused into one piece of glass, so there is nothing to fit and nothing to leak. The tolerance that matters is the height of the inner stem above the chamber floor: if it ends too high, the water will not cover it, and if it ends too low, it will sit in the residue at the bottom. The mouthpiece rim is fire-polished so it has no sharp edge, and the carb hole is punched while the glass is hot so its rim is smooth. The outside is left smooth and clear so the water level can be read at a glance and the smoke seen moving through the chamber. Hammer bubblers rest flat on their base, Sherlock bubblers curve like the pipe in the stories, and sidecar bubblers move the mouthpiece to the side, but the one-piece construction and the small water chamber stay the same in every version. Variants change the shape and the mouthpiece position, not the working principle.
math_proof: The demo treats the water chamber as a cylinder: pi times the chamber radius squared, with a chamber diameter of 45.0 mm, times the water depth of 15.0 mm gives the water volume in millilitres, and the same area times the chamber length of 60.0 mm gives the chamber volume. The bowl cup is a frustum: pi times the bowl depth of 12.0 mm divided by 3, times the sum of the top radius squared, the top radius times the bottom radius, and the bottom radius squared, with a bowl diameter of 18.0 mm and a bottom radius of 3.0 mm. Dividing by 1000 gives cubic centimetres, and multiplying by the packing density of 0.15 grams per cubic centimetre gives the estimated capacity in grams. All numbers come from the specification in this record, and the program prints each result with its unit so the reader can repeat the arithmetic. The reader can check every step with a pocket calculator, because each input is named, each unit is stated, and no hidden constant is used anywhere in the calculation. The computation is run twice and the SHA-256 digests of both runs are printed, confirming the result is deterministic.

First the parts are named and their materials given, so the reader knows what is metal, what is glass, and what is paper. Then the dimensions are stated in millimetres, grams, watts, or litres, so every later number has a source. Then the mechanism is explained step by step, in the order the user actually follows it, so the reader can picture the motion or the flow. The science proof explains the physics behind that mechanism, and the math proof works the arithmetic from the stated dimensions. Finally the demo program computes the same quantities from the same numbers, prints them with units, and runs twice with SHA-256 digests, so the reader can repeat the whole check on their own machine without trusting this record on faith.
print3d: Home 3D printing cannot make every supply in this database, and this section says plainly where the limit falls. A glass bubbler is not 3D-printable at home: no home filament prints glass, and a printed plastic body could not hold the fixed bowl or the fixed inner stem, and would soften near the heat. The printable accessory is a padded carry cradle and a mouthpiece cap for the bubbler. Print the cradle in TPU, which stays flexible and grips the glass without scratching it, with a 0.4 mm nozzle, 0.2 mm layer height, 3 perimeters, and 20 percent gyroid infill, and print the cap in PETG with the same nozzle and layer height at 25 percent infill. Print the cradle flat on its bottom face with no supports, and the cap upright with a brim. Print time (estimate): 1 hour 50 minutes for the cradle and 20 minutes for the cap, at the settings given. Check the finished accessory against the piece it serves before use, and reprint it if the fit is loose, because a holder that does not grip is worse than no holder at all.
problem: The problem this supply solves is practical and narrow: bubbler needs to be prepared or used evenly, reliably, and with ordinary tools, without waste and without guesswork. Before a standard form existed, users improvised, and the result was uneven preparation, spilled material, and parts that wore out or broke. A good supply therefore has to do three things at once: hold the material securely, apply its mechanism evenly across the whole load, and survive repeated use without losing its shape or its edge. It also has to be easy to clean, because residue builds up and changes how it works, and easy to measure, because its dimensions set its capacity. This record states the problem in those terms so the specification, the science proof, and the mathematics can each be checked against it, and so a reader can judge whether the design in the record actually answers the problem it claims to solve.

"""The Bubbler — full working program.

Computes the same quantities as the record demo (bubbler water, bowl, and chamber volumes),
as a documented module with a class and a run() method.
Run: python3 program.py
"""
import hashlib
import math


class SupplyCalculator:
    """Calculator for The Bubbler."""

    def compute(self):
        """Return the computed quantities as a dict."""
        ch_d = 45.0; water_h = 15.0; b_d = 18.0; b_h = 12.0; b_r = 3.0; ch_len = 60.0; rho = 0.15
        water_mm3 = math.pi * (ch_d / 2.0) ** 2 * water_h
        bowl_mm3 = math.pi * b_h / 3.0 * ((b_d / 2.0) ** 2 + (b_d / 2.0) * b_r + b_r * b_r)
        bowl_cm3 = bowl_mm3 / 1000.0
        cap = bowl_cm3 * rho
        chamber_mm3 = math.pi * (ch_d / 2.0) ** 2 * ch_len
        return {"water_volume_mL": round(water_mm3 / 1000.0, 2), "bowl_volume_cm3": round(bowl_cm3, 2), "capacity_g": round(cap, 2), "chamber_volume_mL": round(chamber_mm3 / 1000.0, 2), "bowl_diameter_mm": b_d}

    def run(self):
        """Compute twice, print named results and SHA-256 digests."""
        a = self.compute()
        b = self.compute()
        sa = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(a.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
        sb = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(b.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
        for key in sorted(a):
            print(f"{key}: {a[key]}")
        print(f"Run 1 SHA-256: {sa}")
        print(f"Run 2 SHA-256: {sb}")
        print(f"Deterministic: {'MATCH' if sa == sb else 'MISMATCH'}")
        return a


if __name__ == "__main__":
    SupplyCalculator().run()

science_proof: The bubbler works by shrinking the bong down to one hand. Its water chamber is small, about 24 millilitres in the common example, against about 88 millilitres for a straight tube, so the smoke passes through a short column of water and the cooling is moderate rather than strong. The bowl is small too, about 1.5 cubic centimetres, which sets a small load per bowl, and that is the trade the bubbler makes: it gives up the bong's large chamber and large bowl in exchange for fitting in a pocket. The fixed downstem is a single piece of glass with the body, so there is no joint to leak and no part to lose, but there is also no way to take the stem out for cleaning, which is why bubblers are harder to clean than bongs. The carb hole is the bubbler's clearing mechanism: covering it forces the draw through the bowl and the water, and uncovering it lets fresh air rush in and push the smoke out. Borosilicate glass is used because the piece is carried and handled often, and a glass that tolerates heat and knocks is what survives that use. The numbers in the specification can be checked against this physics: measure the parts, apply the formulas in the math proof, and run the demo program, and the results should agree within the rounding the program reports. If they do not agree, the measurement or the arithmetic is wrong, not the physics, and the reader can find the error by checking one step at a time.
skeptical_analysis: A careful reader should ask what this record does not prove. It does not prove that every example of this supply matches the dimensions given here, because makers vary sizes, materials, and tolerances, and the numbers in this record describe a common example drawn from the cited sources. It does not prove that the supply performs the same way in every hand, because packing, temperature, and technique change the result, and the record describes the mechanism, not a guarantee of outcome. It makes no claim about health, safety, or benefit, and it gives no advice about how much of anything to use. The science proof explains the physics of the mechanism, not a verdict on the practice, and the mathematics checks internal consistency, not real-world performance. Readers should treat the record as a documented, sourced description with a working calculation, check the cited sources themselves, measure any real object they hold, and follow local law. That is the honest limit of what a reference record can claim.
